column1: Is this new story proof in physics that MOND is finished? Https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/technology/is-dark-matter-s-main-rival-theory-dead-the-cassini-spacecraft-and-other-recent-tests-may-invalidate-mond/ar-BB1maqMN?ocid=hpmsn&cvid=31541f6e52e74450 The article is paywalled, so I can't say for sure, but I doubt it. First of all, MOND isn't a “theory” in the same sense as, say, general relativity or even dark matter. It's more of a specific *phenomenological* approach to explain galactic rotation curves without invoking dark matter. That being said, MOND (Modified Newtonian Dynamics) has some very interesting predictions, although its success in matching observations has been… shall we say… mixed. The claim that “MOND is dead” often arises. Frequently, that’s due to new data that doesn’t match MOND’s predictions, particularly regarding observations of galaxy clusters. And in a way, the title of this MSN article is correct. It may very well be that the latest observational/experimental data does indeed invalidate MOND as it was originally formulated. However, this doesn’t necessarily mean the end of MOND as a *concept*. It's a bit like the various versions of string theory: maybe the specific flavor of MOND presented to the scientific community has been refuted by the most recent evidence (the Cassini spacecraft data). However, the *idea* behind MOND, namely that something is wrong with our current understanding of gravity, at least at the scale of galaxies, still stands. Moreover, just as there are a multitude of string theories, so too there are many, *many* modified gravity theories, that is, theories that start with the assumption that Newtonian Dynamics needs to be augmented somehow. Some of these theories do a pretty good job of explaining galactic rotation curves, and some of them even make *different* predictions than the original MOND. It’s an active area of research; I wouldn't be surprised if we saw a new, improved version of MOND in the near future, that takes into account all the more recent observations.

Is the force of gravity instantaneous, or does it take time? Let's consider the implications here. In Newtonian mechanics, gravity *is* instantaneous. The moment the mass of an object changes, the gravitational field instantaneously adjusts everywhere. However, Einsteinian relativity introduces a different perspective. The gravitational field is not a mere “force” but a manifestation of spacetime curvature, and that curvature, like any other aspect of spacetime, propagates at the speed of light. This introduces the concept of gravitational waves, ripples in spacetime that carry information about changes in a gravitational field and their speed of propagation, which is, you guessed it, the speed of light. So, does gravity take time? In the relativistic framework, the answer is unequivocally yes. But let me add a crucial caveat. The effects of any change in the gravitational field will propagate at the speed of light, but this does not mean that the *force* is “late.” In this sense, we are talking about something that has an instantaneous component, and another component that has a delay. Why do Hungarians change Budapest’s name as Bled Attila? Buda is like Hinduism and pest sounds unuseful/harmful animals. I confess, I have no clue whether this is a genuine question or a troll. But let me address it anyway. The naming of Budapest has absolutely nothing to do with Hinduism. Buda, Pest, and Óbuda (Old Buda, the original settlement) are historical names of settlements that predate the unification of the three towns into a single city. As far as I know, the etymology of Buda is likely a personal name, as in, the name of someone, possibly a descendent of Attila the Hun. Pest, on the other hand, likely stems from the Slavic word “peć”, meaning cave. As for the idea that “Pest sounds unuseful/harmful animals”, I’m sure it is a perfectly plausible etymology to the original speakers of Uralic-Altaic languages, but not in Hungarian. Hungarian has its own linguistic quirks, such as a rich system of suffixes and a complete lack of grammatical gender. And, even when it borrows words from other languages it tends to integrate them in a slightly different way. In Hungarian, the ending “-pest” has no meaning. It’s merely a part of the name, just like “-ford” in Oxford.

What is the definition of observation in the double-slit interference experiment of light? Can the visual observation of intelligent creatures determine whether light is a particle or a wave? Observation, in quantum mechanics, is a tricky concept, encompassing far more than just “looking at something.” The double-slit experiment, in particular, is often used to illustrate this. Originally, the experiment demonstrated the wave nature of light, as evidenced by the interference pattern observed when light passed through two slits. However, the situation changes dramatically when we attempt to “observe” which slit the photon goes through. Any measurement that attempts to ascertain the path of the photon, invariably, collapses the wave function, and the interference pattern vanishes. The light then behaves as particles, with a resulting pattern akin to two bright lines rather than the familiar interference fringes. This tells us that “observation” is not merely visual perception, but rather any interaction that reveals “which-path” information, even if it doesn't involve a human eye.  So then, does the visual observation of an intelligent creature change anything? No, not directly. It’s not the mere fact that a conscious being is “looking”, but the physical process of measurement. Let's say we replace the photographic plate with a detector that alerts us which slit the photon passes through. That is observation. Any kind of interaction, like this one, will lead to the collapse of the wave function. In other words, it doesn't matter if the observer is a human, an alien, or a sophisticated piece of machinery. The key is *how* the observation is made, what information is obtained. The underlying physics remains unchanged. The act of measurement, the acquisition of “which-path” (or any other) information is what is crucial, not the presence of consciousness or intelligence. That’s the crux of the matter. Could gravitational redshift account for all cosmological redshift? If it includes all the matter inside the sphere between source and observer (radius)? No. Assuming that we are talking about cosmological redshifts, then the answer is a resounding no, and the reason is simple: Cosmological redshift is *not* a gravitational redshift. It's a *Doppler* redshift that increases linearly with distance, and the cause of this redshift is the expansion of space itself. This expansion is a direct result of Einstein’s field equations, which, as I explained elsewhere, are the be-all and end-all of general relativity. To claim that cosmological redshift is due to gravitation would require a total rewrite of both general relativity and the standard cosmological model, and I can assure you that this is not going to happen. But also… the question is technically ill-posed. Gravitational redshift is a consequence of gravitational potential, which, in turn, is a consequence of the presence of mass. The larger the mass, the larger the gravitational potential, and the larger the redshift. Now, if we could somehow surround our source with a sphere of *infinite* mass, yes, the gravitational potential difference between the source and the observer at infinity would be, well, infinite. But that would require an infinite amount of mass! Moreover, our observer is *not* at infinity. So no, the gravitational redshift would always be finite. And even if it were to be large, it would not look anything like cosmological redshift. For instance, it would be centered on whichever mass generates the gravitational field.
